extracted.intended_audience: scientists (especially those affiliated with or contributing to ESA/Hubble) preparing press releases or working with a press office
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for scientists to prepare and collaborate on press releases about Hubble-related science, covering newsworthiness, visual support, types of releases, procedural collaboration with a press office, and practical science-writing advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor style and content to the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Always tailor the style, level and content of a press release to suit the needs of the press and not the secondary target groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases primarily target journalists; while they may reach decision-makers, other mediators and the public, the writing should be optimized for press use (clear angle, quotable lines, accessible explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate closely with the scientist / Principal Investigator
rubrics_metrics.description: A close collaboration with the scientist (the Principal Investigator) is vital for the practical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PI can supply a short text in simple terms or explain results by phone. Work together to create accurate descriptions and visuals; the PIO will cooperate with the scientist to draft the release and obtain approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Information Officer (PIO) / editorial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Public Information Officer co-operates with the scientist to draft the press release; once approved it may be sent to an internal editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect review for political and scientific issues. The PIO will interface with other institutions' PIOs and may propose co-releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goals of a press release
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release should fulfil three main goals: increase awareness of science and the scientific work process; increase awareness of the organisation; increase awareness of specific scientific projects, instruments or missions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these goals to set the release's objectives and to prioritise content and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Three significant types of releases: News release (focuses on one or more scientific discoveries), Photo release (contains images but no big discovery), Video release (Video News Release for broadcast/web).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the type that fits the content; many written releases are accompanied by high-quality photos and a video. VNRs translate the printed word into the sound and pictures TV newsrooms need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual support is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Images, illustrations and visual design are key factors in successful science communication and often mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with the scientist to create the best possible visuals (artist’s impressions, processed data, videos). Good visuals greatly increase the chance of media uptake given shorter attention spans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing: The story is ‘news’ (the event has just taken place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freshness of the event increases media interest; indicate when the event/result occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance: An issue that has direct or near-direct influence on people’s lives such as fatalities and material damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight concrete impacts or consequences that matter to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proximity: The story has local appeal or local interest (happened in the town or the country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a local angle (institution, researchers, affected region), emphasise it for regional media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Implications: A result that has profound consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain broader consequences or changes to understanding; show why the result matters beyond the specific technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict: Settles a controversial debate or a much-debated topic that contains intrigues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the work addresses a controversy or resolves competing hypotheses, make that framing clear (without sensationalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Human interest: e.g. "Astronomer discovers new galaxies while raising three children and teaching women’s self-defence class in her spare time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal stories, unusual life circumstances of researchers, or emotional hooks can engage broader audiences; use sparingly and honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery: A mysterious phenomenon, quirky details, an unexpected result or a chance discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight unexplained or surprising aspects that draw curiosity, while avoiding misleading implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Major science
rubrics_metrics.description: Major science: Represents a major discovery of a new phenomenon or class of object or an incremental gain in knowledge about a principal field of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise truly novel or significant advances; be clear about the scale of the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — New interesting angle
rubrics_metrics.description: New interesting angle: Twisting an old result in a new way, such as a new, better image that confirms a known result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fresh perspective on existing knowledge can be newsworthy; explain the new element succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — A record
rubrics_metrics.description: A record: First, largest, most distant, fastest, oldest …
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records are easy hooks for headlines — specify the metric and how it compares to prior records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — A sexy topic
rubrics_metrics.description: A sexy topic: Topics that almost always capture public attention (e.g., Solar System topics, space weather, black holes, extrasolar planets, extraterrestrial life, the future of the Earth and Sun and human spaceflight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware such topics attract coverage even if not the strongest science; avoid overhyping weak results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetics: e.g., an exceptionally beautiful image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visually striking imagery can itself justify a release, particularly for outreach and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Publication in a distinguished journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in a distinguished journal: Results published in, for example, Nature or Science tend to attract more interest from journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention prestigious publication venues as part of the context, but couple with accessible explanation of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — Crosslinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Crosslinking: Letting a result piggyback on another news story in a related, parallel or even remotely related field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the result in relation to concurrent stories or trends to increase relevance and media pick-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-or-Not checklist (assess newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think you have a good science result, check with the list of News Criteria above to see if your result is likely to interest the press and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the news criteria as a quick triage before contacting the press office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be proactive
rubrics_metrics.description: If your science fulfils one or more news criteria, do not hesitate to tell the press office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact ESA/Hubble if the story is considered 'hot' — the office can help with drafting, visuals, distribution and media relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in the process
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with the press office to prepare a press release; be prepared to spend time explaining the science and providing proper information to the science communicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active involvement from scientists speeds creation of accurate, clear releases and ensures technical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve other institutions / co-releases
rubrics_metrics.description: The PIO will interface with PIOs of other institutions that have participated in the work, possibly proposing a simultaneous co-release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with collaborators early to agree on timing, wording and visuals for joint announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create images (visuals practically mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sort of eye-catching image or illustration to accompany the press release is practically mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with the press office and scientists to produce appealing and scientifically correct imagery; accompany releases with high-quality photos and videos when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add value with specialist webpages and extras
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists may create more specialised webpages containing additional information, translations, extra images, graphs, technical movies etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental material helps local media and specialist audiences; provide links for journalists to deeper or localized content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare properly (set boundary conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set boundary conditions regarding topic, length, target group and style before drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the angle and constraints early to keep the release focused and appropriate for intended media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your research (answer the six golden questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by answering: What? When? Where? Who? Why? and How? — scan the current literature, review your own writing, mine the web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background research ensures accurate context, avoids repetition of prior coverage and helps identify the best angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure your thinking (brainstorm and find an angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brainstorm the topic to see if elements connect in patterns that help choose your angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise facts and relationships to craft a clear lead and narrative for the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relax during drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to relax and not be overly concerned about the reader when first drafting to remain genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use later edits to refine clarity and audience alignment; initial drafts can be freer to explore phrasing and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent (follow a style guide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow some consistent writing guideline, either personal or organisational (spelling, grammar, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to the organisation’s style guide for consistency across releases; consistency helps editors and journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify (make texts as simple as possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make texts as simple as possible; people do not have time for lengthy explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, concise sentences, avoid jargon, and explain technical terms briefly if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain for a novice reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Match writing to the level of the target group but remember 'the reader knows nothing'; always spell out abbreviations and build explanations from the lowest level without patronising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide necessary background, define acronyms, and avoid assuming specialist knowledge while keeping tone respectful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit and seek outside editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-reading and editing a text always improves its quality; especially valuable if the editor is someone other than the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple editing passes and external reviewers (PIO, colleagues) to catch errors and improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modern writing aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Use features in word processors such as spellcheckers and thesauruses to assist authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage tools to reduce typographical and stylistic errors, but do not rely on them for substantive clarity or accuracy.
